country.comment: Study examines irrigation districts and disadvantaged communities on the San Joaquin Valley floor in California, United States of America.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Abstract, and Author Affiliations; PDF p. 6, Fig 2 caption

effect_estimate.comment: Quantitative descriptive/water-budget results for irrigation districts and unpaired two-sample Wilcoxon test results comparing disadvantaged communities inside vs. outside irrigation district boundaries.
effect_estimate.value: Pre-1914 senior water rights strongly shape agricultural surface water supply: 60% of irrigation districts with pre-1914 water rights hold surface water allocations equal to twice their crop water demand (and up to three times crop irrigation needs), whereas 86% of San Joaquin Valley irrigation districts depend on groundwater for agriculture and 12% rely exclusively on groundwater; using 2001-2015 average surface water deliveries rather than paper allocations increases the number of groundwater-dependent districts by 32%. However, disadvantaged communities inside irrigation district boundaries (ID-DACs, n = 97) do not have significantly better drinking water or socioeconomic outcomes than those outside in groundwater-dependent communities (GDCs, n = 56) on unpaired two-sample Wilcoxon tests: mean Poor Drinking Water Exposure percentile was 83% in ID-DACs vs. 79% in GDCs (p = 0.1363), Threats to Groundwater 56% vs. 55% (p = 0.829), Overall DAC Vulnerability 83% vs. 81% (p = 0.3147), Poverty 83% vs. 84% (p = 0.1166), and 2018 median household income $34,276 vs. $36,450 (p = 0.7893), while ID-DACs had significantly higher Pollution Exposure (81% vs. 74%, p = 0.005413), Pesticide Exposure (83% vs. 77%, p = 0.00965), and smaller mean population (9,899 vs. 20,515, p = 0.003456).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 11, Section 3.2; PDF p. 13, Section 3.3 and Table 1

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at <=2 by observational cross-sectional design (JBI). Rated 1 because the study documents cross-sectional statistical and descriptive spatial associations between legal/institutional variables (historical water rights seniority, district formation era, and LAFCO jurisdictional boundaries) and modeled district water budgets / census-tract drinking-water exposure percentiles without directly observing administrative decision-making or service-delivery processes at the community or household level.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 6-10, Sections 2.1-2.4; PDF pp. 10-16, Sections 3.1-3.4 and Table 1

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines riparian and pre-1914 vs. post-1914 appropriative water rights and 1909 land-value taxation (property), LAFCO irrigation district jurisdictional boundaries vs. unserved GDCs and out-of-district surplus transfers (service_area, discretion), SGMA Groundwater Sustainability Plans and land-repurposing planning (planning), fragmented agricultural vs. domestic water governance across districts/GSAs/SWRCB (institutional_fragmentation), and lack of mandated DAC representation/engagement in irrigation districts prior to SGMA (participation).

study_design.comment: Authors combine GIS boundary overlays, crop evapotranspiration water-budget modeling (WAFR), historical era categorization (1887-2020), cluster analysis of irrigation districts, and cross-sectional two-group Wilcoxon rank-sum comparisons of DACs.
study_design.value: Observational cross-sectional geospatial study combining water-budget modeling, historical era analysis, cluster analysis of irrigation districts, and two-group statistical comparison (unpaired two-sample Wilcoxon test) of disadvantaged communities
